## Preliminary Note on Method

Groupings below are derived from observed patterns in P1 and P2: which items appear in the same contexts, which are contrasted with each other, which share collocational partners, and which participate in similar constructions. No external framework has been imposed. Items are drawn from P1 and P2 only. Where an item fits multiple groups or fits none cleanly, this is noted explicitly.

---

## GROUP 1: Terms used to assert that something is the case as stated

**Label:** Expressions used to affirm that a claim or thing corresponds to what is stated or presented

**Definition:** These expressions are used when a speaker asserts that a proposition is true, that a thing is what it claims to be, or that an account matches reality. They appear in predicative constructions (*egia da*, *egiazkoa da*, *benetakoa da*), in framing devices (*egia esan*, *egiaz*, *benetan*), and in contexts where the speaker is committing to the accuracy of what they are saying. They contrast with expressions in Group 2 (which deny or undermine such correspondence) and with expressions in Group 5 (which hedge rather than affirm).

**Representative expressions:**
- *egia* (truth; P1-1)
- *egia da* (it is true; P1b/C1.2)
- *egiazkoa* (true, genuine; P1-2)
- *benetakoa* (genuine, real; P1-3)
- *benetan* (truly, really, in earnest; P2a-D3.2)
- *egiaz* (truly, in truth; P1b/D1.8)
- *egitan* (truly, in fact, actually; P1b)
- *egia esan* (to tell the truth; C1.1)
- *egia esateko* (to tell the truth, frankly speaking; C1.5)
- *egia da, baina...* (it is true, but...; C1.7) — note: this construction affirms before conceding, so the affirmation function is present even though the construction as a whole introduces qualification

---

## GROUP 2: Terms used to assert that something is false, deceptive, or not what it claims to be

**Label:** Expressions used to deny correspondence between a claim or thing and reality

**Definition:** These expressions are used when a speaker asserts that a proposition is untrue, that a thing is not what it presents itself as, or that a person or document is deceptive. They appear in predicative constructions (*gezurra da*, *faltsua da*), in verbal collocations (*gezur esan*, *gezurra zabaldu*), and in legal and moral contexts where falsity or deception is being named. They contrast directly with Group 1 expressions and frequently appear paired with them (*egia ala gezurra*, *gezurra eta egia bereiztea*).

**Representative expressions:**
- *gezurra* (lie, falsehood; P1-4)
- *faltsua* (false, fake, deceitful; P1-5)
- *gezurra da* (that is a lie; C4.3)
- *gezur esan* (to tell a lie; P2a-D4.7)
- *gezurretan ari da* (he/she is lying; C4.2)
- *gezurrezko* / *gezurrezkoa* (false, based on lies; P2a-D4.1/D4.2)
- *gezurti* / *gezurtia* (liar; P2a-D4.3/D4.4)
- *faltsukeria* (deceitfulness, duplicity; P2a-D5.1)
- *faltsuki* (falsely, deceitfully; P2a-D5.2)
- *gezurra zabaldu* (to spread a lie; C4.7)
- *gezurra eta egia nahastu* (to mix truth and lies; C4.4)
- *lekuko faltsua* (false witness; C5.4)
- *dokumentu faltsua aurkeztu* (to present a forged document; C5.2)
- *gezurra txuri* (white lie; C4.9)

## GROUP 3: Terms used in contexts of formal or procedural verification

**Label:** Expressions used when the truth or validity of something is being officially confirmed, tested, or demonstrated

## AMBIGUOUS OR OVERLAPPING ITEMS

The following items show patterns of use that place them in more than one group, or that do not fit cleanly into any single group identified above.

---

**benetakoa** (genuine, real; P1-3)

Fits Group 1 (affirming correspondence with reality), Group 6 (authenticity of objects), and Group 7 (genuine character of persons). The term is used across all three contexts in the data, and no single context dominates. The adverbial *benetan* (truly, really) fits most naturally in Group 1, while *benetakotasuna* (authenticity) fits most naturally in Group 6.

---

**jatorra** (genuine, authentic, decent; P1-15)

Fits Group 6 (authenticity of objects or versions) and Group 7 (honest character of persons). In colloquial usage the person-evaluation sense predominates; in some contexts it describes authentic versions of things. The pairing *jatorra eta zintzoa* (C15.2) places it firmly in Group 7, while *jatorrizkoa* (original; P1-21) represents a related but distinct form that fits Group 6 more cleanly.

---

**egiazkoa** (true, genuine; P1-2)

Fits Group 1 (affirming truth of claims), Group 6 (authenticity of objects: *egiazko argazkia*, *egiazko historia*), and Group 7 (genuine character: *egiazko adiskidea*, *egiazko maitasuna*). The *egiazko-* attributive form is highly productive and appears across all three contexts. No single group captures all its uses.

---

**zuzena** (correct, right, straight, just; P1-6)

Fits Group 9 (correctness of statements and procedures) and also appears in moral evaluation of persons and conduct (*bide zuzena hartu*, *zuzena eta bidezkoa*). The moral and procedural senses are both well-attested. The derivative *zuzendaritza* (management, directorate; P2a-D6.5) and *zuzendaria* (director; P2a-D6.6) operate in an institutional domain that does not fit any of the groups identified here; these forms are noted as not fitting cleanly.

---

**balioa** (value, worth, validity; P1-12)

The *balio-* root covers at least two distinct usage patterns: formal/legal validity (Group 4: *baliozkoa*, *baliogabea*) and worth or value in a broader sense (moral value, aesthetic value, economic value: *balio etikoa*, *balio estetikoa*, *balio sinbolikoa*, *balio unibertsalak*). The broader value uses do not fit Group 4 and do not fit any other group identified here. They are noted as not fitting cleanly. The *baliatu* (to make use of) and *baliagarria* (useful) branch noted in P1b as peripheral extensions similarly does not fit any group.

---

**egia mingarria** (painful truth; P1b)

This collocation frames truth as an experiential quality with affective consequences. It fits Group 1 in that it asserts something is true, but the evaluative dimension (painful, difficult to hear) does not correspond to any of the usage patterns that define the groups above. It is noted as not fitting cleanly.

---

**egia osoa** (the whole truth; P1b) and **egia erdiak** (half-truths; P1b)

These collocations involve quantification of truth rather than simple assertion or denial. *Egia osoa* fits Group 1 (affirming complete truthfulness) and Group 3 (legal oath contexts). *Egia erdiak* fits Group 2 in that it describes misleading statements, but it is distinct from outright lying (*gezurra*). Neither fits any single group cleanly.

---

**ustez** (supposedly, allegedly, presumably; P1-30)

Fits Group 5 (hedging epistemic status). However, in journalistic usage *ustez* specifically attributes a claim to a source or to general belief rather than simply marking uncertainty, which is a slightly different function from *itxuraz* (which marks appearance-based inference). Both are placed in Group 5, but the distinction between them is preserved here.

---

**zintzoa** and *fidagarria* overlap

Both are used in evaluating persons, but *zintzoa* (Group 7) concerns intrinsic character, while *fidagarria* (Group 8) concerns whether a person or source can be relied upon for information. The pairing *zintzo eta leial* (honest and loyal) is a character description; *iturri fidagarria* (reliable source) is an epistemic evaluation. In some everyday uses the distinction is not sharp.

## 1. ATTRIBUTION

### Pattern
Predicate-nominal or predicate-adjectival construction: **[Noun/Proposition] + [truth-term] + da**
The truth-term occupies predicate position; the copula *da* (3sg present of *izan*) follows. Word order is flexible but predicate-before-copula is canonical.

### Examples
- *Egia da hori.* → Egia da hori. → "That is true."
- *Egiazkoa da agiri hori.* → Egiazkoa da agiri hori. → "That document is genuine."

### Notes
The copula *da* is obligatory; the truth-term does not inflect for the subject. Both nominal (*egia*) and adjectival (*egiazkoa*, *benetakoa*, *baliozkoa*, *sinesgarria*, *zuzena*) bases participate in this pattern without structural difference.

---

## 2. NEGATIVE ATTRIBUTION

### Pattern
Negation particle **ez** precedes the copula: **[Noun/Proposition] + ez + da + [truth-term]**
Alternatively, the negative particle may precede the entire predicate complex.

### Examples
- *Ez da egia hori.* → Ez da egia hori. → "That is not true."
- *Ez da sinesgarria.* → Ez da sinesgarria. → "It is not credible."

### Notes
*Ez* immediately precedes the finite verb (*da*); the truth-term remains in predicate position. This is the standard negation pattern for all copular attributions in Basque and applies uniformly across the truth-domain vocabulary.

---

## 3. ADNOMINAL MODIFICATION

### Pattern
Attributive modifier precedes the noun in its **indefinite form** (article *-a* dropped): **[truth-term-zko / truth-term-ko] + [Noun]**
The suffixes *-zko* and *-ko* derive relational adjectives from nominals; the resulting form is invariant before the head noun.

### Examples
- *Egiazko lekukotasuna* → Egiazko lekukotasuna → "True/genuine testimony"
- *Benetako arazoa* → Benetako arazoa → "The real problem"

### Notes
Basque attributive modifiers are pre-nominal and appear without the definite article *-a*. The forms *egiazko*, *benetako*, *gezurrezko*, *baliozko*, *jatorrizko*, and *itxurazko* all follow this pattern. The head noun carries the definiteness and case marking.

---

## 4. BECOME / INCHOATIVE

### Pattern
Verb **bihurtu** ("to become, to turn into") or **bihurtu da** with a truth-domain nominal or adjectival as complement: **[Subject] + [truth-term] + bihurtu da**
Alternatively, some roots form inchoatives via **-tu** suffixation directly (*okertu*, *zilegitu*).

### Examples
- *Egia bihurtu da.* → Egia bihurtu da. → "It has become true / It turned out to be true."
- *Okertu egin da gauza hori.* → Okertu egin da gauza hori. → "That thing has gone wrong."

### Notes
The periphrastic *bihurtu* construction is the general inchoative strategy and applies broadly. The suffixed *-tu* inchoative is lexically restricted: *okertu* (to go wrong, become crooked) is well-attested; *zilegitu* (to become legitimate) is marginal. No *-tu* inchoative from *egia* or *gezurra* is attested.

---

## 5. CAUSATIVE

### Pattern
The suffix **-arazi** attaches to the verbal stem to form a causative: **[Verb-stem] + -arazi**
For truth-domain verbs: *egiaztarazi* (to cause to verify), *frogararazi* (to cause to prove). Alternatively, periphrastic causatives use **eragin** or **behartu** with an infinitival complement.

### Examples
- *Egiaztarazi zion.* → Egiaztarazi zion. → "He/she made him/her verify it / caused it to be verified."
- *Egia esan eragin zion.* → Egia esan eragin zion. → "He/she made him/her tell the truth."

### Notes
Morphological *-arazi* causatives are grammatically productive in Basque but are relatively low-frequency for truth-domain verbs in the data; periphrastic causatives with *eragin* or *behartu* + infinitive are more commonly attested in this domain. No causative from nominal bases (*egia*, *gezurra*) via *-arazi* is documented in the data.

---

## 6. ABSTRACT NOMINALIZATION

### Pattern
Suffix **-tasun** attaches to an adjectival base to form an abstract nominal denoting the property: **[Adjective] + -tasun + -a** (definite)
This is the primary and fully productive abstract nominalization pattern across the truth-domain vocabulary.

### Examples
- *Zintzotasuna* → Zintzotasuna → "Honesty, sincerity, integrity"
- *Fidagarritasuna* → Fidagarritasuna → "Reliability, trustworthiness"

### Notes
The *-tasun* suffix applies uniformly to all adjectival bases in the data: *egiazkotasuna*, *benetakotasuna*, *faltsutasuna*, *zuzentasuna*, *zehaztasuna*, *sinesgarritasuna*, *jatortasuna*, *antzekotasuna*, *baliogabetasuna*. A secondary pattern, the *-pen* suffix, derives result-oriented nominals from verbal stems (*egiaztapen*, *frogapen*, *zehaztapen*).

---

## 7. AGENTIVE NOMINALIZATION

### Pattern
Suffix **-ti** attaches to a nominal root to form a person noun denoting habitual or characteristic engagement: **[Root] + -ti + -a** (definite)
This pattern is attested for the falsehood domain. For the truth-telling domain, no parallel *-ti* form is documented; the function is expressed periphrastically.

### Examples
- *Gezurtia* → Gezurtia → "The liar" (habitual liar; from *gezur-* + *-ti* + *-a*)
- *Egia esaten duena* → Egia esaten duena → "The one who tells the truth" (periphrastic; no single-word form attested)

### Notes
The *-ti* agentive is asymmetric in this domain: *gezurti* (liar) is a fully lexicalized common word, but no corresponding *egiazkoti* or *egiati* (truth-teller) is attested. The truth-telling agent is expressed periphrastically via relative clauses (*egia esaten duena*) or by character adjectives (*zintzoa*, *jatorra*) rather than by a dedicated agentive nominal.

---

## 8. VERBAL NOMINALIZATION (action / process)

### Pattern
Suffix **-tze** + definite **-a** attaches to the verbal stem to form a verbal noun denoting the action or process: **[Verb-stem] + -tze + -a**

### Examples
- *Egiaztatzea* → Egiaztatzea → "The verifying, verification (as process)"
- *Frogatzea* → Frogatzea → "The proving, demonstration (as process)"

### Notes
This pattern is distinct from the *-pen* result nominal (§6 secondary pattern) in that *-tze* nominals denote the ongoing process or act, while *-pen* nominals (*egiaztapen*, *frogapen*) denote the result or outcome. Both are productive across the verification sub-domain. Verbal nouns in *-tze* function as syntactic subjects and objects freely (*frogatzea zaila da*, "proving it is difficult"; *frogatzeko zama*, "burden of proof").

## 9. PRIVATIVE / NEGATED-PROPERTY CONSTRUCTION

### Pattern
Two competing strategies are attested:
**(a)** Suffix **-gabe** attaches to a nominal root: **[Root] + -gabe + -a** → property-lacking nominal
**(b)** **ezin** (impossibility marker) precedes the verbal stem: **[Verb-stem] + ezin + -a** → "impossible to [verb]"

### Examples
- *Baliogabea* → Baliogabea → "Invalid, null, without value" (*balio* + *-gabe* + *-a*)
- *Frogaezina* → Frogaezina → "Unprovable, impossible to prove" (*froga* + *ezin* + *-a*)

### Notes
The *-gabe* privative is productive for nominal roots (*baliogabea*, *egigabea*) and for verbal stems (*zehaztugabea*, *egiaztatu gabe*). The *ezin* construction is specific to verbal roots and expresses impossibility rather than mere absence (*egiaztaezina*, *frogaezina*). The antonym of *-garri* adjectivals (§10 below) is preferentially formed with *-gaitz* rather than *-gabe* (*fidagaitza*, *sineskaitza*).

---

## 10. POTENTIAL / WORTHY-OF ADJECTIVAL

### Pattern
Suffix **-garri** attaches to a verbal stem to form an adjectival meaning "worthy of" or "capable of being [verbed]": **[Verb-stem] + -garri + -a**
The negative counterpart uses **-gaitz** (difficult, resistant): **[Verb-stem] + -gaitz + -a**

### Examples
- *Frogagarria* → Frogagarria → "Provable, demonstrable"
- *Fidagaitza* → Fidagaitza → "Unreliable, hard to trust"

### Notes
The *-garri* / *-gaitz* pair is productive across the epistemic sub-domain: *egiaztagarria* (verifiable) / *egiaztaezina* (unverifiable, via *ezin*); *frogagarria* / *frogaezina*; *fidagarria* / *fidagaitza*; *sinesgarria* / *sineskaitza*. The negative of *-garri* forms uses *-gaitz* (or *-kaitz*) rather than *-gabe*, a pattern consistent across all attested examples in the data.
